title: Only extrinsic value is income: separate it from intrinsic value
summary: When you track P&L on short options, split the premium into intrinsic and extrinsic value. Only the extrinsic value is true premium or income. Intrinsic value is capital: money you owe or money returned to you. Counting the whole premium as income overstates the yield, most of all on in-the-money strikes.

steps.caption: The stock trades at $100. We sell an in-the-money $90 call against 100 shares.
The $90 strike is $10 below the market. That $10 is intrinsic value.
The legs: long stock and a short call. The call premium has two parts.
At expiry the stock is called away at $90. The $10 intrinsic part only returns capital; it is not income.
The maximum profit equals the extrinsic value only. That is the true premium.
Extrinsic value decays to zero by expiry. Track it as income; track intrinsic as capital.

takeaways: Separate intrinsic from extrinsic value when you attribute P&L.
Only extrinsic value is income from selling options.
Intrinsic value is capital that you owe or that is returned to you.
caveats: The transcript says 'covered put'; the rule applies to covered calls, cash-secured puts and other short options alike.
The speaker promotes a waitlist and tools on his website. They are promotional and not verified here.
